articles.title: Meta agrees to heavy restrictions on teen users in major lawsuit settlement
articles.summary: Meta agreed to settle claims brought by state attorneys general across the country saying it misled users about the safety of its apps for teens.
articles.body: Meta settled its latest kids online safety trial with a group of 29 state attorneys general, sparing it from the remainder of a trial that could have cost it hundreds of billions of dollars. Under the terms of the settlement, which resolves claims by a larger group of 47 states and several districts and territories, Meta agreed to come up with an age assurance standard that is subject to independent testing, and must have a false positive rate no higher than 10 percent for users aged 16 to 17, and 3 percent for users aged 13 to 15. The company also agreed to give teens the option to turn off personalized feeds, meaning that they won’t be shown content based on Meta’s recommendation algorithm, and Meta will suspend push notifications for teens between 10 PM and 7 AM unless parents disable those restrictions, as well as limit teens to two hours of Meta app usage per day (with exceptions for messaging and “longform content”). Meta will also agree to pay $17.1 billion to states over a period of 10 years. The company outlined its obligations in a blog post, noting that $5.3 billion of this money will only be paid out if YouTube and TikTok implement their own daily time limits and each pay an equivalent amount to that figure. The agreement requires Meta to try to link accounts owned by a single user to prevent circumvention of its new rules, and provide an appeals process for users. Users who say they’re over 18 but don’t complete the age assurance test within two weeks will have restrictions on their accounts meant to “restrict potential adult bad actors” from contacting teens, and be served “content recommendations inspired by Age Appropriate Experiences.” Meta will also disable push notifications during school hours for teens, unless their parents allow them. It will also implement “productive pauses” at 60 and 90 minutes of cumulative daily use of its apps, and give “a Clear and Conspicuous notice” after 15 minutes of use. The company also agreed to disable filters that simulate cosmetic procedures for teens, and likes on posts to prevent social comparison. It says it will not make false or misleading statements about the efficacy of its safety features. Another part of the settlement references “Age Signals from Google and Apple Operating Systems and App Stores,” and says Meta will incorporate reliable signals shared by those companies into its age assurance framework. This is something Meta has been lobbying states and Congress to force Apple and Google to do. “Our new Time Limit commitments, Night Mode features and usage limits during school hours set the right path forward for our whole industry, but this framework will only work if all our peers join us,” Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. “Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away.”

articles.title: Fed seen a bit more likely to hike after inflation data
articles.summary: Aug 26 (Reuters) - The case for a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike gained a little steam on Wednesday after a government report showed inflation in July wa...
articles.body:
Aug 26 (Reuters) - The case for a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike gained a little steam on Wednesday after a government ‌report showed inflation in July was a touch stronger than ‌economists had expected.

The 12-month gain in the personal consumption expenditures price index, which the ​Fed targets at 2%, edged up to 3.7% last month from 3.6% in the month prior, the Commerce Department said. Core PCE inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy and is seen as ‌an indicator of underlying ⁠inflation pressures, was 3.3% from a year earlier, no better than it had been in June.

The Fed has ⁠held its policy rate steady in the 3.50%-3.75% range since December, and though Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has vowed to end above-target inflation ​he has ​not given any indication about whether ​he believes it will recede ‌without interest-rate hikes. Wednesday's data do not show it is, in conflict with earlier reports that did show a slowdown in consumer price inflation over the last couple of months.

"The United States still has an inflation problem," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy ‌Federal Credit Union. "The latest data give (Warsh) time ​to wait and see, but he ​has to be more clear ​about what he's watching closely and what it ‌would take for him to hike ​rates."

Fed funds futures ​prices now reflect about a 44% probability of a September Fed rate hike, versus about 36% immediately before, and show traders ​are fully convinced ‌that the Fed will have raised the policy rate by ​the end of the year.

(Reporting by Ann Saphir, Editing ​by Louise Heavens and Chizu Nomiyama )

articles.body:
The WNBA’s Chicago Sky have banned former pro basketball player Enes Kanter Freedom from the team’s arena after he got into an altercation with one of its players over the weekend.

Sky owner Michael Alter told reporters Tuesday that Freedom will not be permitted inside the Wintrust Arena moving forward “unless sometime in the future, he’s able to prove to us to our satisfaction that he is able to abide by our rules without being a potential threat,” according to The Associated Press.

During a game Sunday, Freedom engaged in a verbal altercation with Chicago’s Natasha Cloud, an incident that led him to be ejected from the game.

Freedom has thrust himself into the center of a debate about the WNBA’s eligibility rules by saying he declared for the league’s draft earlier this month.

The former player and others have pressed the association to “define what a woman is,” amid a broader debate national Republicans are having about transgender women playing women’s sports.

There are no transgender or male athletes competing in the WNBA.

Freedom wrote on social media after he was ejected from the game he was tossed for “supporting women.”

“It was pretty clear to us that his purpose of coming here was trying to be provocative and just see how much attention he could get and stir up and create,” Alter said.

articles.title: Meta settles social media addiction trial with states for up to $17B
articles.summary: Meta and a coalition of state attorneys general reached a settlement in the high-profile trial accusing the company of designing its platforms to be addictive for young users, according to court filings published Wednesday. The proposed settlement, later announced by California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D), will require Meta to make various changes to its…
articles.body:
Meta and a coalition of state attorneys general reached a settlement in the high-profile trial accusing the company of designing its platforms to be addictive for young users, according to court filings published Wednesday.

The proposed settlement, later announced by California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D), will require Meta to make various changes to its apps, such as Facebook and Instagram, and pay up to $17 billion to the states over 10 years.

Changes include default daily time limits for users under 18, as well as restrictions on use and notifications at night or during the school day, according to Bonta.

“Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms — and will do it within months. We are talking about time limits, stopping notifications during school, a block on the app during critical overnight hours, bans on plastic surgery filters, and so much more,” Bonta wrote in a press release Wednesday.

The proposed settlement with 52 state attorneys general will need to be approved by a judge, and settles claims filed by 47 states.

California and 28 other states sued Meta in 2023, alleging the Facebook and Instagram parent company designed and implemented harmful features that encourage “excessive use” in teens and younger children.

The suit also accused Meta of misleading the public about their apps’ mental and physical health risks and routinely collecting the data of users younger than 13 without parental consent.

The complaint at the center of this trial was originally filed by 29 states, but only covered the first four: California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey. The states were seeking a $1.4 trillion penalty.

The settlement will effectively stop the trial in California, during which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg was expected to take stand

Meta’s chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, said the settlement includes a “new set of rules governing teens’ use of social media” and called on other industry competitors to also implement a similar framework.

“The framework we’ve negotiated will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platform,” Mahoney said in an emailed statement. “This framework will only work if all our peers join us. Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution.”

Mahoney specifically called on TikTok and YouTube to follow “Meta’s lead.”

As part of the settlement, Meta agreed to set a default daily time limit of two hours for users under 18 that can only be lifted by a parent, Bonta said. If other social media firms agree to similar terms, the daily time limit will drop to one hour.

The company will also institute a nighttime block between midnight and 6 a.m. for users under 18. Like the daily limit, this can only be lifted by a parent and should other social media firms agree, the nighttime block will change to 10 p.m. to 7 a.m.

Notifications will also be blocked for minors from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m. and during the school day.

In addition to time limits, Meta will roll out an “enhanced” way for teens to report potentially harmful content. Meta will be required to respond to 90 percent of those reports within six hours.

A display of the number of likes or reactions will also be banned for minors, along with the plastic surgery image filters.

Meta currently allows users 13 and older and will be maintaining age assurance measures to detect users under 18 and remove users under 13.

Attorneys general from across the country celebrated the settlement Wednesday morning.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) said Big Tech “is finally being held accountable for the harm” on kids’ mental health and safety. The settlement will dish out more than $500 million to New Jersey, she added.

Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman (R) said the Bluegrass State is expected to receive $358 million under the settlement, but added, “While Meta is certainly paying for its conduct, this was never just about the money.”

Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser (D) said his state will receive nearly $615 million over the next nine years, which will go towards youth mental health and safety initiatives.

The landmark trial came just months after Meta lost in two other kids safety trials in California and New Mexico.

The cases focused on the platform design rather than the content posted to social media, making it easier for prosecutors to get around Section 230, which protects technology firms from being held legally liable for third-party or user content.

Section 230 has largely shielded several social media firms in lawsuits related to the content posted on their platforms.

articles.title: CISA confirms hackers targeted over 100 US water systems during July | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The federal cyber agency's warning comes amid a wave of suspected Iran-backed cyberattacks targeting critical water systems across the United States.
articles.body:
U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA said it has observed cyberattacks targeting over 100 internet-exposed systems across the U.S. water and wastewater sector, amid a wave of hacks targeting American critical infrastructure.

The number of affected systems provides new context to the scale of the ongoing cyberattacks targeting water providers in Michigan, Minnesota, and at least five other states.

The federal agency, which oversees cybersecurity defense and critical infrastructure protections, said in an advisory that the attacks have largely targeted programmable logic controllers (PLCs), which are used to control physical systems and machinery across water providers, energy systems, and other parts of critical infrastructure.

In recent weeks, hackers have targeted PLCs made by several manufacturers, including Rockwell, Schneider Electric , and more recently, Siemens . CISA previously said that the cyberattacks are relying in part on AI tools that rely on public information to develop scripts capable of targeting vulnerable Siemens PLCs.

The intrusions have had little effect on water or waste water supplies to local communities, but have resulted in outages and disruption as incident responders investigate the breaches. CISA previously reported that some of the intrusions allowed hackers to modify affected PLCs to disable shutdown processes and alarms, potentially creating “unsafe conditions” without notifying the affected operators.

Many of the affected communities are in rural or isolated areas, where disruption to critical infrastructure systems can affect a large area of people.

Reports citing senior American officials say that U.S. intelligence believes Iran is likely behind the largely opportunistic attacks on water providers, likely in response to the U.S. and Israel-led war against Iran, but officials have fallen short of a concrete attribution.

The intrusions have sparked broader concerns about the cybersecurity and resiliency of critical infrastructure across the United States.

U.S. officials have warned in recent years that hackers working for China have been planting destructive malware on critical infrastructure ready to activate as a distraction in the event of an anticipated Chinese invasion of Taiwan. Russia has also been linked to several cyberattacks on water providers, and power and energy grids, across Europe as part of a growing campaign seen as aimed at testing the NATO alliance.

articles.title: RFK Jr. responds to Shapiro over measles-related deaths
articles.summary: Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. shot back at Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) on social media after the governor blamed him and the Trump administration for playing a part in the measles outbreaks that led to two deaths in his state. Pennsylvania on Tuesday confirmed two deaths in unvaccinated individuals…
articles.body:
Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. shot back at Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) on social media after the governor blamed him and the Trump administration for playing a part in the measles outbreaks that led to two deaths in his state.

Pennsylvania on Tuesday confirmed two deaths in unvaccinated individuals after they contracted measles, the first such deaths reported this year.

In a press conference, Shapiro blamed the Trump administration for spreading misinformation that led to declining vaccination rates.

“There’s real-life consequences to scaring people and not relying on actual doctors and actual medical professionals to provide unbiased information to parents so that we can make reasonable decisions for our kids,” said Shapiro.

Kennedy, one of the nation’s top vaccine skeptics prior to becoming secretary, defended himself and his previously stated claims on social media.

“During our phone conversation, Governor Shapiro also accused me of promoting vaccine misinformation. When I asked him for an example, he was unable to provide one, but this did not deter him from publicly repeating that accusation during his press event,” Kennedy wrote on the social media platform X.

“As I told him, HHS does not tolerate misinformation by any employee. I offered to point to hundreds of instances of vaccine misinformation by the Biden administration about which I had never heard him complain,” he added.

The secretary also repeated the claim that the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine “contained fetal tissue,” pointing to previous testimony from Stanley Plotkin, the developer of the rubella vaccine.

As organizations like the American Academy of Pediatrics have clarified, vaccines do not contain fetal cells. Some vaccines are developed by growing viruses in a cell line derived from two aborted fetuses from the 1960s, but as these lines are ongoing no more aborted fetuses are required for vaccine development today. The purification process removes fetal tissue from the final product.

articles.title: US seizes domains of Chinese botnet used to hack NASA, Justice Department, and the Senate | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The FBI has seized domains associated with a botnet that allowed Chinese-backed hackers to breach several U.S. government departments.
articles.body:
The FBI has seized a series of domains that were used by a large-scale botnet to coordinate and launch China-backed cyberattacks against American targets.

According to the Justice Department’s statement on Wednesday, the seizures of the botnet’s domains deny the operators access to the platforms. The botnet was allegedly used by the Chinese government to break into computers across the United States, including systems at hospitals, defense contractors, and several federal government departments.

Prosecutors said the China state-sponsored group, known as QTFY, was run by a Chinese company called Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Tech, which created and operated the botnet of thousands of compromised internet-connected devices. The botnet aimed to serve as obfuscation networks, which hide the malicious traffic of hackers to make their activity more difficult to detect.

Per the Justice Department, QTFY offers computer hacking services to its customers, who include Chinese government hackers working for the Ministry of State Security, and allows them to use the botnet.

The hacks date back to 2018, and affected NASA, the Federal Reserve, and the Departments of Energy, Justice, and Health and Human Services. The U.S. Senate was compromised as recently as 2026, according to the government’s affidavit seeking a court order to seize the botnet’s domains filed earlier this week.

The Justice Department said that the domain seizures made the botnet and its command and control servers “inoperable,” as the domains were hardcoded into the botnet’s code, and were critical for the botnet’s communication and essential operations.

Network giant Lumen said in a blog post that it had observed the hackers profiling and targeting government agencies, the defense and aerospace sectors, and others for the past year, and shared threat intelligence with the FBI.

articles.title: FDA approves groundbreaking new pancreatic cancer drug
articles.summary: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Wednesday approved a treatment for advanced pancreatic cancer, offering new life-extending care for patients with one of the most aggressive forms of cancer. The once-daily pill, called daraxonrasib and manufactured by Revolution Medicines, will be sold under the brand name Rasonque. It was approved for patients who already tried…
articles.body:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Wednesday approved a treatment for advanced pancreatic cancer, offering new life-extending care for patients with one of the most aggressive forms of cancer.

The once-daily pill, called daraxonrasib and manufactured by Revolution Medicines , will be sold under the brand name Rasonque. It was approved for patients who already tried one line of therapy, or if they are not candidates for initial chemotherapy.

The drug is not a cure. But it’s the first real option for extending the life of patients diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.

Pancreatic cancer accounts for a disproportionately high share of cancer deaths, despite representing only about 3 percent of all cancer diagnoses. The aggressive disease is typically detected late, and there have been historically limited treatment options that do little to extend a patient’s life. The five-year survival rate is only about 8 percent.

“The FDA approval of Rasonque is a monumental step forward for patients with pancreatic cancer and for the oncology field,” said Mark Goldsmith, chief executive officer and chair of Revolution Medicines, in a statement.

“For the first time, patients have an approved targeted medicine designed to directly inhibit the main cause of pancreatic cancer, RAS, which has been one of the most intractable disease targets since its discovery decades ago,” Goldsmith said.

Daraxonrasib attacks the underlying genetic causes of pancreatic cancer. It targets a group of proteins called RAS, which when mutated are a key driver of tumor growth in most patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

Patients with advanced pancreatic cancer who received the drug during a key clinical trial saw a median overall survival of 13 months, compared to just six months for patients who were offered standard chemotherapy.

The trial found daraxonrasib reduced the risk of death by 60 percent compared with chemotherapy.

“Today’s approval provides a critical new option for patients facing an extraordinarily difficult and historically hard-to-treat cancer. It is our fundamental duty to deliver more cures and meaningful treatments to patients as quickly as possible,” acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas said in a statement, adding that the approval was a “groundbreaking milestone.”

Revolution Medicines did not immediately announce how much it planned to charge for the drug.

The FDA granted Rasonque a priority review voucher, which is intended to help accelerate the review of therapies that address national public health priorities.

The company opened an FDA-cleared expanded access program in May and has since distributed the drug to more than 2,000 patients through participating academic cancer centers and community oncology practices.

The most common adverse reactions in patients were rash, diarrhea, stomatitis, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, edema, decreased appetite and hemorrhage.

One of the most high-profile clinical trial participants is former Sen. Ben Sasse (R-Neb.), who announced in December he had been diagnosed with Stage 4 pancreatic cancer. Sasse told The New York Times in April that he credits the drug with shrinking his tumors, but the cancer has likely spread to so many other parts of his body “that it’s probably just not something you can ever catch up on.”

articles.title: Trump sends Saudi Arabia nuclear deal to Congress
articles.summary: President Trump’s administration sent a nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia that would allow the kingdom to enrich uranium to Congress this week, kick-starting a congressional review process required under the Atomic Energy Act. However, President Trump’s retroactive condition for the deal — that it will only move forward if Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham…
articles.body:
President Trump’s administration sent a nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia that would allow the kingdom to enrich uranium to Congress this week, kick-starting a congressional review process required under the Atomic Energy Act.

However, President Trump’s retroactive condition for the deal — that it will only move forward if Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham Accords — has not changed, an administration official told The Hill on Wednesday.

The 30-year agreement, which the U.S. announced last month, would allow U.S. companies to develop Saudi Arabia’s civil nuclear infrastructure.

The White House submission starts the review period under Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act. The agreement does not need two-thirds approval in the Senate, but the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Senate Foreign Relations Committee have a chance to contest it during a 90-day review period.

If Congress does not pass a joint resolution to reject the deal during that period, it can take effect. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the president sending the agreement to Congress.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed the deal on July 22. The agreement faced immediate backlash from nonproliferation experts, supporters of Israel and some congressional Democrats, warning the accord could pave the way for Saudi Arabia to build a nuclear weapon.

Some of those lawmakers raised the same concerns this week.

Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), the co-chair of the bicameral Nuclear Weapons and Arms Control Working Group, urged Congress to reject the agreement, stating it does not possess the “most stringent safeguards against the development” of nuclear weapons.

“If the Trump administration wants to stop a Saudi bomb, it should require the nonproliferation Gold Standard, which would ban enrichment and reprocessing and require International Atomic Energy Agency additional protocol safeguards in Saudi Arabia. If Riyadh did not want a bomb, it would accept the Gold Standard,” Markey said in a statement on Wednesday. “But the opposite is happening.”

articles.title: Medical device maker Boston Scientific says a cyberattack is causing a 'global disruption' to its operations | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The company won't say if medical devices are affected or if any customer data was exfiltrated.
articles.body:
A cyberattack on U.S. medical device maker Boston Scientific is causing an ongoing “global disruption” to its operations, according to a federal regulatory filing on Wednesday, the latest healthtech giant to face a cyberattack in recent weeks.

The Massachusetts-based company, which makes medically implanted devices like pacemakers and defibrillators, confirmed in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that on Tuesday it began experiencing “disruptions and limitations of access” to its IT systems and business applications critical for its operations.

Boston Scientific said the cyberattack has affected its ability to ship and process orders, but has not said whether the disruption extends to customers with medical devices and implants.

When asked by TechCrunch, Boston Scientific spokesperson Chanel Hastings shared the company’s public statement , but would not comment on whether patients are affected by the cyberattack, say what steps patients should take, or answer questions about the nature of the incident.

Boston Scientific treats around 48 million patients a year, according to its website .

The company’s public statement said that its investigation is ongoing and that a timeline for its restoring its systems is not yet known.

It’s not clear what caused the cyberattack at Boston Scientific. Local media in Ireland reported that thousands of staff across Boston Scientific’s campus in Cork were sent home on Tuesday after network communications were cut across the company.

The company is the latest health technology company to have been hacked this year, including medical device makers Abbott Laboratories and Medtronic. Earlier this year, Iranian-backed hackers were blamed for a cyberattack on U.S. medical device maker Stryker, which allowed the hackers to remotely wipe tens of thousands of employee devices across its Windows network by abusing a centralized device management portal provided by Microsoft.

According to public internet records, Boston Scientific relies largely on Microsoft and Amazon Web Services for its corporate infrastructure.

articles.title: Bessent’s ‘Treasury Twist’ Has Wall Street War-Gaming a Shift in Borrowing Strategy
articles.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s more activist style of managing the nation’s debt has Wall Street war-gaming a potentially bigger shift in the governme...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's more activist style of managing the nation's debt has Wall Street war-gaming a potentially bigger shift in the government's borrowing strategy over the coming months.

One radical option would be to cut sales of long-dated bonds, according to Deutsche Bank AG, Morgan Stanley and Citigroup Inc. More likely, the Treasury could signal at its Nov. 4 quarterly refunding that future increases in borrowing will be done via bills and shorter-maturity notes, while further expanding buybacks to ease pressure on long-term yields.

The rethink shows how Bessent's actions are bringing uncertainty to a policy long known for being "regular and predictable." Bank of America strategists, led by Meghan Swiber, said it signals the start of "a new regime" as officials take a more "activist" role in shaping the market.

Bessent's moves have "effectively made the November refunding announcement more of a wildcard than otherwise would have been the case," said Ian Lyngen, head of US rates strategy at BMO Capital Markets. "Reductions to bond auction sizes can no longer be ruled out."

For now, Bessent has ruled out changes to the regular auction program, saying that Treasury will stick with its current schedule until at least the next refunding. But a revamped buyback program announced last week, which he dubbed a "Treasury twist," raised the stakes around the November announcement for the $31 trillion Treasury market.

The expanded buybacks are unlikely to deliver a meaningful transformation of the government's debt maturity on their own. Unlike the Federal Reserve, Treasury cannot create money to finance its purchases, meaning buybacks must ultimately be funded with additional issuance, most likely bills, or with cash from the Treasury General Account.

"Expanded buybacks themselves are likely just a bridge until they get to November refunding," said Martin Tobias, a rates strategist at Morgan Stanley. "The market-moving event ultimately will be the manner with which Treasury goes about shortening the weighted-average maturity."

Tobias expects the Treasury will gradually increase sales of shorter-dated notes, while keeping longer-maturity sales steady. However, the risk of outright cuts to long-end auctions has gone up over the last week, he said.

articles.title: Iran puts Europe on notice as US shifts to economic warfare
articles.summary: Iran’s recent saber-rattling against Bulgaria has renewed questions over how much it’s willing to directly attack Europe in an effort to deter U.S. allies from aiding war efforts against Tehran. articles.body:
Iran’s recent saber-rattling against Bulgaria has renewed questions over how much it’s willing to directly attack Europe in an effort to deter U.S. allies from aiding war efforts against Tehran.

Bulgaria, among Iran’s biggest trading partners in Eastern Europe, is among the European countries Iran considered striking if President Trump escalated the war, The Financial Times reported last week. That’s due to both its south-eastern location on the continent and two U.S. Air Force KC-135 refueling planes using one of its bases to support Operation Epic Fury.

After Bulgarian officials announced the departure of those planes over the weekend, Iran on Monday issued its latest warning to NATO members that allow their territory to be a jumping off point for American or Israeli military action against the regime, saying it “has the right to target the point of origin and source of any act of aggression against” it.

Iran has made similar threats to the United Kingdom, with a drone striking a British airbase in Cyprus in March. That same month, Iran fired two ballistic missiles at the remote U.K.-U.S. base in the Indian Ocean known as Diego Garcia. And Turkey in March said NATO’s air defenses had intercepted several ballistic missiles launched from Iran.

While Iran clearly wants to maintain the perception that it’s willing and capable of striking Europe, analysts aren’t convinced it really wants to invite NATO more fully into the fight.

“What’s the bang they get for that buck?” said Alan Eyre, a former head of the Iran office at the

U.S. Consulate in Dubai, now with the Middle East Institute.

“Iran right now is in a fight for its life. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is leading it, and their target selection is going to be based on optimal utility, and that could well encompass targets in Europe,” he told The Hill, but added that he doesn’t think such a scenario is likely.

“I don’t think the juice is worth the squeeze in terms of antagonizing NATO. . . . I don’t think that attacking European targets gets them anything extra than attacking [Gulf] targets doesn’t get them,” Eyre said.

David Cattler, a senior fellow with the Center for European Policy Analysis, likewise said that an Iranian strike on a NATO ally would be a major escalation but a bad strategic trade for Tehran, as “that would probably transform Europeans who largely have sought distance from the Iran war into active participants against” the regime.

Trump has repeatedly complained that NATO members aren’t doing enough to help clear the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran’s military moved to close almost immediately after the U.S. and Israel launched their surprise attack in February.

Cattler said the more immediate issue is Iranian coercion.

“The reality is Tehran doesn’t need to fire a missile at Bulgaria to achieve an effect. Threatening the countries that provide the bases, logistic support, access to the United States is itself an attempt to raise the price of supporting Washington in an attempt to weaken allied cohesion,” Cattle told The Hill.

Iran’s foreign ministry on Monday declared that while it has “no issue with the Bulgarian people,” it stressed that “any action regarded as supporting U.S. and Israeli military aggression against Iran constitutes, under international law, participation in an act of aggression.”

The regime was referring to the Friday departure of two U.S. Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, air-to-air refueling tankers from Bulgarian territory, which had been temporarily deployed to Bezmer Air Base in support of the U.S.’s Operation Epic Fury.

Al Jazeera reported this week that Bulgarians living around Bezmer were well aware of the threats, quoting a woman at a local grocery shop who said, “I pray to God that our village won’t be attacked.”

The regime previously warned the Balkan nation, which is roughly 2,000 miles from Iran and shares a border with Turkey, against allowing Washington to use its airbases during the conflict.

Bulgaria is likely within striking range for Iran, closer than the island of Diego Garcia, which is some 2,350 miles away from Iran. The targeting of Diego Garcia earlier this spring with two Iranian missiles — one that failed in flight and one shot down — changed Europe’s calculations around Tehran’s ability and willingness to hit locations outside the Gulf region, said Cattler.

“Iran’s demonstrated substantially greater reach than many Europeans had previously had to factor into their defense planning,” Cattler told The Hill. “Even though they didn’t hit, NATO did take note of that and described that development as relevant to allied security.”

He pointed to NATO helping Turkey defend against Iranian ballistic missiles earlier in the war.

“That’s, again, just a sign of both NATO preparedness and the defensive response,” Cattler said.

The U.S., meanwhile, has taken a new tactic in attempting to bring Iran to its knees, with Trump warning last week that he would hit Iran with an “Economic D-Day.” That was followed by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement on Monday of “Operation Economic Outcast,” in which the U.S. is asking nations across the world to sever financial ties with Tehran or risk being cut out of the U.S. dollar system.

Both Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have said they are prepared to return to military options if necessary, though there are mounting concerns about the U.S.’s dwindling weapons stockpiles.

Iran has remained defiant in the face of the economic chokehold, with Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh on Tuesday telling state television that Tehran was “fully prepared for the U.S. sanctions.”

“Our defense is no longer defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack,” the Iranian official said, according to Reuters .

Eyre said it’s “wildly improbable” that Operation Economic Outcast will cause Iran to recalibrate its negotiating stance to meet America’s demands.

“The fallacy the U.S. government is making is that they think that by making the lives of ordinary Iranians more wretched, that will translate into effective political pressure on the Iranian leadership. It won’t,” he said.

“If, in fact, the economic pain from the naval blockade or from Economic Outcast reaches a certain point, the Iranian leadership is not going to capitulate. They’re going to escalate.”

Trump’s latest tactic of an economic chokehold follows the June memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran, which fell apart last month after Tehran attacked shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Both sides accused each other of violating the interim deal, leading to a shuttering of the vital waterway by Iran, a renewed U.S. blockade on Iranian ports, and a brief resumption in military strikes.

Weeks of diplomatic efforts, including negotiations between Oman and Iran to set up shipping lanes in the strait, have failed to yield a breakthrough for peace.

Eyre said the only reason he sees Iran attacking European targets is for the effect it would have on financial markets, given how the war has shifted to an economic battlefield for now.

“Not letting President Trump and the administration off the hook in terms of increasing economic pressure — the price of gasoline going up, price of diesel going up, the bond markets running over the Treasury secretary. To optimize that, they might well choose European targets,” he said.

“But then again, they get most of that anyway by attacking [Gilf] targets. Any renewal of kinetic action on the part of Iran is going to tweak the markets.”

articles.title: All the ways Instagram and Facebook are changing for teens
articles.summary: Meta has agreed to make sweeping changes for teens on Instagram and Facebook as part of a child safety settlement.
articles.body: Meta just agreed to make sweeping changes for teens as part of a child safety settlement reached with attorneys general across the US. Under the agreement, Meta must apply new safeguards across Instagram and Facebook that will change how teens interact with the social media platforms, as well as restrict their use during certain times. The settlement stems from a nationwide lawsuit alleging Meta, Google, TikTok, and Snap failed to protect children and made their platforms “addictive” by design. A group of 51 US states and territories signed the agreement, including New York, New Jersey, California, Nevada, South Carolina, Washington, Illinois, and many more. Most of these protections are required to remain in place for at least 10 years. The changes are coming to Facebook and Instagram in all US states except for New Mexico, which is in the middle of a legal battle with Meta, and Florida, which has banned kids under 14 from creating social media accounts. Texas also reached a separate settlement with Meta with similar requirements. Here’s a list of the biggest changes: * A non-personalized feed option: In four months, Facebook and Instagram must give teens the “reasonably accessible” option of a default feed that isn’t personalized by Meta’s recommendation engine. Meta will occasionally send teens reminders about this option, and parents will also be able to set it as their child’s default setting. * Age assurance: Meta has agreed to ramp up efforts to identify and apply restrictions to underage users on the platform. Under the settlement, Meta must either continue to develop its own age assurance standard or adopt a third-party option. The method must evaluate whether a user is under 13, so they can be removed from the platform, or identify if someone is aged 13 to 17, in which case they would receive teen account protections. New users who haven’t yet been evaluated by Meta’s system will receive teen protections by default. Meta must also adhere to data minimization policies, implement a process for users to appeal their status as a minor, and have its age assurance system reviewed by an independent auditor. * Two-hour time limit: Teens will only be able to use Instagram and Facebook — cumulatively — for two hours per day, unless the limit is turned off by a parent. Meta will apply the time limit not only across both apps, but across a user’s alternate account if it detects one. As noted in the settlement agreement, time spent consuming videos or audio more than 22 minutes long, messaging, or using an app’s settings won’t count toward the limit, which will reset at 12AM each day. * Persistent prompts: Within four months, Meta is required to show teens prompts every 15 minutes that they continually scroll on Instagram and Facebook to prevent “excessive, mindless, or unintended” usage. The platforms will also send prompts after 60 minutes and 90 minutes. An example of the notification included in the settlement shows a message saying, “You’ve scrolled for a while. Try exploring something new,” with a prompt for users to view content related to other topics and to review their algorithm. Parents can change this setting to be less or more restrictive. * Nighttime restrictions: Meta will block teens from accessing most of Facebook and Instagram between midnight and 6AM. During this time, teens can’t post on either platform or view feeds, stories, reels, or scroll through their Explore page. Teens will still be able to access messaging features and account settings at night, and parents, again, can adjust the setting. * Muted notifications during the school day: Teens won’t receive push notifications by default between 8AM and 3PM, except for “direct messages and alerts about their account security or safety,” unless the setting is changed by a parent. * Toggle off autoplay: Teens will get the option to turn off autoplay, which means they’ll have to tap or swipe their screen to view content, rather than Instagram or Facebook playing it as soon as it appears on their screen. * No more visible likes: Facebook and Instagram will begin hiding the number of likes and reactions on teens’ posts by default, and will stop showing them on other posts as well. * Limited access to beauty filters: Meta already blocks teens from using cosmetic surgery filters, but it will now restrict their access to “extreme makeup” filters as well. The agreement says this doesn’t include effects that make users look like a fantasy character, an animal, or effects that “entertain users by distorting their appearance.” It also doesn’t include filters that “smooth skin or alter appearance in ways that can be achieved by ordinary makeup techniques.” [Image: Here’s what Meta’s persistent notifications might look like every 15, 60, and 90 minutes of scrolling. Meta has committed to keeping many of its existing safety standards as well. That means placing all teens into more private accounts by default, preventing “potentially suspicious adults” from messaging them, and making it more difficult for adults to find, follow, or interact with young users. The company also says it will keep its age-appropriate content restrictions, which hide posts containing nudity, sexual content, strong language, or risky stunts from teens. Meta is calling on TikTok and YouTube to make similar changes, saying “these protections will only be truly effective if we work with our peers.” It must pay $17.1 billion to states over 10 years, but says it will pay $5.3 billion of this sum only if TikTok and YouTube pay the same amount, as well as implement a daily time limit for teens, add restrictions at night, and roll out age assurance measures.

articles.title: Tap-to-pay charity scam can cost you thousands
articles.summary: A tap-to-pay charity scam is turning small $15 or $20 donations into charges of nearly $5,000, with victims losing thousands before they notice.
articles.body: Tap to pay has become one of my favorite modern conveniences. I use it all the time. In fact, I rarely need to pull out a physical wallet anymore because contactless payments are accepted in so many places. There's a security advantage, too. Mobile wallets can use tokenization or virtual card numbers, so your actual card number does not need to pass directly to a merchant during a transaction. That makes what's happening with a tap-to-pay charity scam especially frustrating. Criminals are taking a technology designed to make paying easier and using a moment of distraction to turn a small donation into a potentially massive charge. You may think you're giving $5 or $20 to a good cause. Then you check your account and discover hundreds or even thousands of dollars are gone. Here's how the scam works and what you can do to protect your money. APPLE PAY TEXT SCAM THREATENS $8,250 LOSS IN 35 MINUTES New! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward. Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com. How the tap-to-pay charity scam works The setup can feel completely ordinary. You're leaving a store, walking through a busy shopping area or heading through a public event. Someone approaches you and claims to be raising money for a youth group, school fundraiser or another cause. They ask for a small donation. Maybe you agree to $5. Maybe you offer $20. Then they tell you they can accept tap to pay. That's when you need to pay very close attention. The scammer enters a different amount One version of the scam involves the solicitor entering a much larger amount into a smartphone or payment reader before you tap your phone or card. You think you're approving $20. The payment screen may actually say $2,000. If you tap without carefully checking that amount, you could authorize the larger transaction. Brentwood police warned in January 2026 about a version involving people approaching shoppers outside stores for small donations. Police said victims could be charged significantly more than expected after using tap to pay, Square or Cash App. Some victims lost thousands of dollars The numbers can get ugly fast. The Washington State Attorney General issued a warning after receiving reports involving solicitors near the Seattle waterfront. In one case, a person agreed to donate $15 and later discovered a $4,800 charge. Another person agreed to give $20 and later found a charge of nearly $5,000. Those examples show why you should never treat the final tap as a formality. Never hand a stranger your unlocked phone There's another risk worth keeping in mind. If someone claims the transaction failed and asks to take your phone to help, end the transaction. A scammer does not need to take your phone for the inflated-payment scheme to work. However, handing over an unlocked phone creates a much bigger security problem. Depending on your settings, that person may be able to reach email, messages, payment apps or financial information. I would never hand an unlocked phone to a stranger during any financial transaction. Why tap-to-pay security may not stop this scam Tap to pay itself remains a secure way to make legitimate purchases. The weakness here involves what you approve. If a scammer puts $2,000 on the payment screen and you authenticate that transaction, the payment system sees an approved purchase. The criminal is counting on you to skip one very important step: reading the amount before tapping. We use contactless payments so frequently that the gesture can become automatic. Pull out the phone. Authenticate. Tap. Walk away. That routine gives a scammer an opening. CyberGuy has previously covered how quickly mobile payment scams can turn into serious financial losses through services such as Venmo, Zelle and Cash App. How to protect yourself from a tap-to-pay charity scam You do not need to stop using tap-to-pay. I certainly don't plan to. Instead, change how you handle unexpected payment requests. Keep your phone in your hands Never give a stranger your unlocked phone to complete or troubleshoot a payment. If something supposedly went wrong with a transaction, cancel it and move on. When your financial information is involved, you should stay in control of your device from beginning to end. Read the amount before you tap This may be the single most important habit. Stop for a second and look at the amount displayed on the merchant's phone or payment terminal. Do this before your phone or card goes anywhere near the reader. If you agreed to donate $10, make sure the screen says $10. The FTC also recommends reviewing your financial statements after making donations to confirm you were charged only the amount you intended. NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS Avoid high-pressure donations A legitimate cause will still exist five minutes from now. If someone tells you that you need to donate immediately, I would walk away. Scammers often rely on pressure because they do not want you thinking too carefully about the request. The FTC specifically advises people against letting fundraisers rush them into making a donation. Research the charity yourself Ask for the organization's name, then look it up independently. Do not rely on a website, QR code or social media account the solicitor hands you. Search for the charity yourself and check whether it is registered. Look for independent reviews and see how the organization says donations should be made. The FTC recommends researching unfamiliar charities before sending money. Use the charity's official donation channel If the cause sounds worthwhile, you can still donate. Go directly to the organization's official website after you have verified it. That gives you time to confirm who will receive your money without someone standing over you waiting for a tap. Turn on bank and card alerts I'm a big fan of account alerts because they can tell you the moment something happens with your money. Turn on notifications for card purchases and withdrawals. Also consider alerts for transfers or other significant account activity. If you intended to donate $20 and immediately get an alert showing $2,000, you can contact your financial institution right away. Lock down your payment and banking apps Check the security settings inside apps such as Venmo, Cash App, PayPal and your bank's mobile app. Enable Face ID, fingerprint authentication or a separate PIN when the app offers those protections. That creates another barrier if someone ever gets access to your unlocked phone. What to do if you already fell for the scam If you spot an inflated charge or realize you approved far more than you intended, move quickly. The sooner you respond, the sooner your bank can tell you what options are available. 1) Contact your bank or card issuer immediately Call the bank or card issuer connected to the transaction. Explain exactly what happened. Tell them how much you agreed to pay and how much was actually charged. Ask whether the transaction can be stopped, disputed or reversed. If your banking app allows it, consider locking the affected card while you investigate. Brentwood police specifically advise suspected victims of this scam to contact their bank or card issuer immediately. 2) Save evidence of what happened Take screenshots of the transaction and save any payment confirmations. Write down where the encounter happened and approximately what time it occurred. Also record the merchant name shown with the charge. Those details can help your bank or law enforcement investigate. 3) Check every financial account on your phone If the scammer ever handled your unlocked phone, review the financial apps installed on it. Look for unfamiliar transfers or purchases. Then check whether anyone changed your email address, phone number or other account information. Continue watching those accounts over the following days because suspicious activity may appear later. 4) Change passwords if your phone left your hands If a stranger had access to your unlocked device, change passwords for sensitive accounts that may have been exposed. I would start with your primary email account because criminals can use email to reset passwords elsewhere. Then secure banking and payment accounts. Use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account, and turn on multifactor authentication wherever it is available. HOW FLORIDA RETIREE LOST $200K IN FAKE PAYPAL REFUND SCAM 5) Strengthen your phone security Make sure your phone requires Face ID, fingerprint authentication or a strong passcode. Also protect sensitive apps when your device offers that option. The goal is to keep someone from turning a few seconds with your unlocked phone into access to your financial life. 6) Use strong antivirus software Antivirus software will not reverse an inflated tap-to-pay transaction. However, it becomes much more relevant if the scammer convinced you to click a link, visit a website or download something. Strong antivirus protection can help detect malicious software and warn you about dangerous links used in follow-up scams. I recommend running trusted security protection across your devices and keeping it updated. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 7) Reduce the personal information scammers can find Fraudsters often come back for a second attempt. If they learn your name, phone number or other personal details, they can combine that information with data already available online to make the next scam more convincing. Data brokers and people-search sites can expose personal information about you. You can remove much of this information yourself. However, the process can take time and information may reappear. A data removal service can automate many of those removal requests and continue checking for your information. It cannot erase information a criminal already obtained. Still, reducing your online footprint gives scammers less material to work with. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. 8) Consider identity theft protection If someone gained access to sensitive information on your phone, you may want an additional set of eyes watching for signs of fraud. Identity theft protection services can monitor for suspicious activity and alert you when certain personal information appears in places it should not. Some services also provide recovery assistance if your identity gets misused. That can be especially useful if you believe the incident exposed more than a payment card. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com. 9) Consider freezing your credit A fraudulent tap-to-pay charge by itself does not automatically mean someone can open credit in your name. However, the situation changes if a scammer also obtained sensitive personal information that could be used for identity theft. In that case, consider placing a credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze can make it harder for a criminal to open a new credit account in your name. 10) Report the scam If you lost money, report what happened. Contact local law enforcement when appropriate, especially if the amount is significant or the same solicitors appear to be targeting other people. You can also report fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If the person claimed to represent a charity, consider contacting your state attorney general or charity regulator as well. The safest way to donate with your phone I still like mobile wallets and I still plan to use tap to pay. The technology gives us convenience along with useful payment protections. What changes for me is how I handle a stranger asking for a quick donation. I want to know exactly who is getting my money before I approve anything. If I decide the cause deserves support, I can look up the organization later and donate directly through its verified website. That approach removes the pressure and gives me time to make sure my money reaches the people I intended to help. Kurt's key takeaways Tap to pay remains one of my favorite ways to check out. I like the speed and I like the added security mobile wallets can provide. Still, technology cannot protect you from every number you personally approve. That's what makes this scam effective. Most of us have become so comfortable tapping that we barely think about the final transaction screen. I want that habit to change. Before you tap, look at the amount. If a stranger is asking for a donation, give yourself time to verify the organization first. And if anyone asks to take your unlocked phone during the process, my answer would be an immediate no. Your generosity should reach the cause you chose, rather than a scammer counting on a few distracted seconds. Would you still tap your phone to donate to someone who approached you in public after seeing how easily a small gift can become a four-figure charge? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: General Mills removes artificial colors from US cereals
articles.summary: General Mills said Wednesday that it has ended the use of artificial coloring in its United States cereal portfolio with intentions to remove the dyes from its full U.S. retail portfolio by the end of 2027. In a press release, the company stated that 90 percent of General Mills’s U.S. retail portfolio had made the…
articles.body:
General Mills said Wednesday that it has ended the use of artificial coloring in its United States cereal portfolio with intentions to remove the dyes from its full U.S. retail portfolio by the end of 2027.

In a press release , the company stated that 90 percent of General Mills’s U.S. retail portfolio had made the transition while all of its cereal already removed certified colors.

“This achievement reflects how we are evolving with consumer needs while continuing to offer food that tastes great, delivers quality and provides value,” Big C Cereal President at General Mills Bethany Quam said.

The company also stated that it will be launching “twice as many new products” for consumers with “different needs and preferences … including more protein and fiber options, along with even more new foods featuring familiar ingredients that consumers recognize and trust.”

WK Kellogg Co. reported a similar move on Aug. 6 to mandate an accelerated timeline in the company to remove artificial dyes from products.

The push comes more than a year after former Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Commissioner Marty Makary enacted regulation to phase out petroleum-based food dyes in U.S. food products. Makary, at the time, linked the dyes to ADHD, obesity, diabetes, insulin resistance and cancer.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. echoed Makary’s points, calling the dyes “poisonous compounds” that endanger children’s health and development, citing limited evidence of potential health risks.

In place of synthetic dyes, food-makers can use natural hues made from beets, algae, crushed insects, as well as pigments from purple sweet potatoes, radishes and red cabbage.

Makary said the FDA would be initiating a plan to revoke the authorization of the synthetic food colorings Citrus Red 2 and Orange B with further plans to remove other synthetic dyes off the market by the end of 2026, including Red Dye 40, Yellow No. 5, Yellow No. 6, Blue No. 1, Blue No. 2 and Green No. 3.

Trix, a General Mills cereal, contained three FDA-targeted dyes — Red Dye 40, Blue No. 1 and Yellow No. 6 — before the company phased them out.

Other food companies that have made voluntary moves to produce naturally colored products are PepsiCo, Conagra, McCormick, J.M. Smucker Co., Hershey Co. and Kraft Heinz Co.

articles.title: Lobbyists go to work for Canada tariff carveouts
articles.summary: The US levies on wine, dairy and more affect only a sliver of goods, but they could have an outsize impact on select states.
articles.body:
Companies that do business with Canada, and the lawmakers who represent them, are ramping up their lobbying for carveouts from new US tariffs on Canada .

The US levies on wine, dairy and more affect only a sliver of goods, but they could have an outsize impact on select states, particularly when combined with Canada's retaliatory tariffs . It's unclear whether US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will grant any of the exemption requests — neither the US nor Canada wants to show "holes in the tariff wall," in the words of Baker Donelson's Lee Smith, a former Commerce Department official.

While both sides try to hold firm, lawmakers continue to nudge Greer. Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., previously wrote to him expressing concern over imports like road salt . Now, those conversations have taken on a fresh urgency, with Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, urging Greer to scrap the new tariffs entirely .

"Any business that has a Washington lobbyist on speed dial is looking for a carveout, and I'm telling all of those businesses: 'You go, girl,'" the Detroit Regional Chamber of Commerce's Sandy Baruah said.

One industry representative put it another way: "I've been telling everyone I talk to for the past year-and-a-half, 'Don't use any of the E-words.' You're just going to get laughed out of the room if you come in and say, 'I need an exception or exclusion.'"

With US and Canadian officials still at odds, some companies are increasingly concerned that the two countries may not ink a trade deal before President Donald Trump leaves office. Consumer Technology Association Vice President of International Trade Ed Brzytwa posited that the time between rollouts could spur "a downward spiral" of retaliation.

"I don't know how this is going to evolve in a mutually productive fashion," Brzytwa said.

Already, the US is eyeing additional trade penalties on Canada. White & Case's David Bond predicted that officials would raise the tariffs already in effect, as Trump threatened Monday, "rather than trying to expand the scope of the tariffs to include other products."

Canada's levies, announced weeks before the midterms, are poised to hit vulnerable Republicans particularly hard. Bond pointed to purple states like Wisconsin, which exports dairy, and Maine, which exports seafood.

"The Canadian tactic is to try to get Congress to lobby on their behalf," Mayer Brown's Warren Payne said. He predicted that the strategy would prove less effective than it has in the past: "It is not the same Congress as the first Trump administration, and they're just not getting the level of support from Congress that they got the first time around."

articles.title: Bill Gates: AI will either be ‘greatest equalizer’ or ‘worst source of injustice’
articles.summary: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates argued Tuesday that AI will either be the “greatest equalizer ever invented” or the “worst source of injustice,” calling for society to act quickly to prepare for the technology’s impacts. In an essay published on his website Gates Notes, the tech billionaire suggested that leaders are not adequately confronting the challenges…
articles.body:
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates argued Tuesday that AI will either be the “greatest equalizer ever invented” or the “worst source of injustice,” calling for society to act quickly to prepare for the technology’s impacts.

In an essay published on his website Gates Notes, the tech billionaire suggested that leaders are not adequately confronting the challenges posed by AI.

“Even under the best circumstances, the transition to this new AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history,” he wrote, adding, “There is no plan to ease the entry into the AI era.”

He pointed to the labor market, noting that AI will likely disrupt jobs across numerous industries and move faster through the economy than earlier technological transitions.

“We have to think now about how to reduce job losses so that everyone can share in the prosperity that AI creates,” he said. “Waiting until people are already displaced or underemployed will be too late. AI is a structural challenge to the way our economy is organized, and it requires thinking and action now.”

Gates warned that AI is creating new cybersecurity risks and threatens to replace human relationships. However, he also underscored the potential benefits from the technology, such as quicker advancements in healthcare and boosts to agriculture in low-income countries.

He argued that “maximizing the benefits” of AI is “just as important as minimizing the harms.”

“If people see how AI makes their lives easier, it will help build the public trust that is necessary for managing the harder parts of the transition,” Gates said. “If the first thing AI does in most people’s lives is take away their job, those who are already skeptical about it will outright reject it.”

This comes at a moment when AI is increasingly unpopular. A recent survey from Pew Research found that 52 percent of respondents said they are more concerned than excited about the technology, while just 9 percent said they are more excited than concerned.

Gates called for both domestic and international frameworks on AI, in addition to setting aside certain jobs for humans and establishing new taxes on AI tokens and robots.

“This unprecedented technology demands an unprecedented global response,” he added. “If we get it right, the payoff for humanity will be phenomenal and the world will be a more equitable place.”

articles.title: FedEx Commits $400 Million to Indian Air Cargo Growth With Delhi, Mumbai Hubs
articles.summary: The facilities will add more than 500,000 square feet of air cargo space as India looks to more than double its national handling capacity by 2030.
articles.body:
FedEx is investing $150 million to develop an integrated air cargo hub at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport, with completion expected within 12 to 18 months.

The proposed 230,000-square-foot facility, located within the airport's 50-acre GMR Cargo City complex, will bring the company's international gateway and pickup-and-delivery operations under one roof. Once operational, it is expected to increase FedEx 's processing capacity in Delhi from 600 packages per hour to 5,000 on average, with scope to scale up further.

The logistics giant plans to introduce extensive automation at the facility, including automated sortation systems and high-speed X-ray screening equipment, in an effort to enable shipments to be processed more efficiently while increasing throughput.

The groundbreaking ceremony for the facility was held in the national capital on Tuesday attended by India's civil aviation minister Kinjarapu Rammohan Naidu.

Delhi Airport is India's leading air cargo hub , moving 1 million metric tons of freight per year, according to Naidu.

" India is a critical market in our global network, with north and east India playing an important role in the country's growing trade and economic opportunity," said Kami Viswanathan, president of FedEx Middle East, Indian Subcontinent and Africa (MEISA) in a statement. "Strengthening our presence in Delhi will enhance connectivity across these markets and support businesses as they grow and expand. It reflects our long-term confidence in India and our commitment to investing in the capacity and capabilities needed to support the country's evolving trade needs."

The Delhi hub is one three air gateways FedEx operates in the country. Delhi supports the northern and eastern parts of India, complementing a hub in Bengaluru in the south and Mumbai on the west coast.

In February, the logistics provider announced a long-term investment of $250 million in a new cargo hub at Navi Mumbai International Airport, bringing the combined commitment in the new Indian hubs to $400 million. That month, FedEx and the airport broke ground on the fully automated 300,000-square-foot facility.

The regional consolidation and distribution hub is planned to commence with an initial handling capacity of approximately 500,000 metric tons annually, scaling in phases to around 2.6 million metric tons in its final development stage.

articles.title: Meta reaches $18B deal on kids’ use of Facebook, Instagram: 4 takeaways
articles.summary: A landmark settlement between Meta and attorneys general across the country will see the technology giant pay more than $18 billion to states but also roll out several changes to better protect kids and teens on its Facebook and Instagram platforms. The settlement proposal, which awaits a judge’s approval, will end the high-profile trial in…
articles.body:
A landmark settlement between Meta and attorneys general across the country will see the technology giant pay more than $18 billion to states but also roll out several changes to better protect kids and teens on its Facebook and Instagram platforms.

The settlement proposal, which awaits a judge’s approval, will end the high-profile trial in California, but it will alter kids’ and teens’ experiences with Meta, and potentially other platforms, for at least the next decade.

It builds upon years of pressure on Meta to better prevent children and teens from experiencing negative mental and physical consequences caused by the apps’ designs.

Here are four takeaways on a momentous day in the tech world.

The settlement, announced Wednesday, effectively ends the trial in California centered on allegations the Instagram and Facebook parent company knowingly designed its platforms to keep minor users addicted and misled the public about the apps’ risks.

The lawsuit was first filed in 2023 by a group of 29 state attorneys general, but the settlement expanded to 47 U.S. states, three territories and the District of Columbia after Meta said it approached “nearly every state” to collaborate on a safety framework.

The settlement includes a monetary payment of up to $17 billion dispersed to the states over the next decade. The money will go to state efforts to prevent or reduce mental health or other harms associated with social media use.

Several state attorneys estimated how much their state could receive from the payout, with California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) stating between $1.5 billion and $2.1 billion for the state.

Separately, Meta will pay Texas more than $1 billion over similar allegations , bringing the company’s total sum to just more than $18 billion.

The states argued in court that Meta designed and implemented harmful features that encourage “excessive use” of Facebook and Instagram by teens and younger children. They alleged Meta also misled the public about the mental and physical health risks associated with its apps and routinely collected the data of users younger than 13 without parental consent.

The trial lasted just a week and was expected to feature testimony from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. While the CEO will not testify, the California court did hear from the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, on Tuesday.

Just a day before the settlement, Mosseri told the court Meta introduced a “Take A Break” pop-up feature on Instagram in 2021 to help teens control their time spent on the app, but it had lower uptake than the executive hoped.

As for the two states not included in the settlement, New Mexico already fought Meta in court and won last March. The company was ordered to pay the state $567 million.

In Florida, Attorney General James Uthmeier (R) said the payout was “peanuts” compared to Meta’s alleged harms and vowed to “ see them at trial .”

While the payment is a small part of Meta’s revenue last year of $201 billion, the biggest implications lie in the platform changes that are poised to significantly influence young users’ experiences on Instagram or Facebook.

Meta said it hopes the changes create a national framework for other social media firms to agree on.

Under the settlement, the company will set a default daily time limit of two hours for users under 18 that can only be lifted by a parent. If other social media firms agree to similar terms, the daily time limit will drop to one hour.

The company will also institute a nighttime block between midnight and 6 a.m. for users under 18. Like the daily limit, this can only be lifted by a parent, and should other social media firms agree, the nighttime block will change to cover the hours of 10 p.m. to 7 a.m.

Notifications for users under 18 will also be blocked from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m. and during the school day — 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. from Aug. 15 to June 15, Bonta’s office said.

Teen users will also receive prompts every 15 minutes they continuously spend on Facebook or Instagram, along with prompts when daily usage hits 60 or 90 minutes.

Minors will also no longer be able to see the number of likes and reactions on both their own and others’ posts by default, while cosmetic surgery and extreme makeup filters will be disabled.

Meta currently allows users 13 and older but said Wednesday it will invest in stronger age assurance technology to detect users who may lie about being under 18 and remove users under 13.

Teens will also be able to choose a “non-algorithmic feed” as a default, rather than the typical personalized feeds that are generated by a users’ activity on the platforms.

The majority of the terms are required to remain in place for 10 years, though the time and night limitations will start with a five-year commitment, according to Meta. Should other tech firms sign the agreement, it will extend this commitment to 10 years.

These features build upon the Teen Account program, which was rolled out in 2024 for all users under 18. Existing features include age-appropriate content restrictions and defaulted private accounts.

The deal could have implications for other social media companies

In announcing the settlement, Meta specifically called out YouTube and TikTok to “join” the company in adopting what it calls a “new standard” for kids online safety.

In an open letter , Meta argued the benefits of its new standards will only be “truly effective” if other industry players follow the same standard, putting public pressure on its rivals to make a deal.

“All platforms should empower parents and support teens in these ways because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another. For meaningful progress to happen, we urge our peers to join us,” Meta wrote in the open letter .

It is not clear how the other companies will react, given they are facing their own legal challenges over similar allegations.

Meta’s deal allows it to position itself

The settlement allows Meta to both avoid the rest of the trial, including Zuckerberg’s testimony, but also position itself as a new leader in the kids online safety space.

It comes just months after Meta lost in two other kids online safety trials earlier this year.

A day after New Mexico’s victory against Meta last March, a California jury determined in a separate case that Meta and YouTube were negligent in their design or operation of the platforms and ordered the companies to pay a combined $6 million.

The back-to-back verdicts sent a warning shot to Big Tech , as it was the first time juries found the social media platforms liable for their impact on kids and teens. Legal experts told The Hill the successful verdicts could pave the way for similar outcomes in other trials.

Since then, several social media firms began settling similar cases before they hit the court. Weeks before a trial slated for June, Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snapchat settled a suit alleging the firms intentionally designed platforms to keep kids engaged, prompting mental health issues.

“This massive settlement shows how terrified Meta and Mark Zuckerberg are of accountability in open court,” Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), the Senate co-authors of the landmark Kids Online Safety Act, said in a statement.

“Between devastating evidence that was emerging in the trial and pending legislation in California, Mark Zuckerberg saw the hammer coming down. Meta’s decision to settle is proof that the prospect of paying real money works,” Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of the nonprofit Common Sense Media, said in a statement following the settlement news.
