articles.title: Early government projection showed thousands of Americans at risk of harmful exposure after East Palestine train derailment
articles.summary: An early government projection on the exposure to toxic chemicals following the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio, train derailment indicated that the incident could have put thousands of Americans at risk, according to documents obtained by a watchdog group. The incident, which became a political flashpoint, spilled chemicals including vinyl chloride, which is used to make plastic, into…
articles.body:
An early government projection on the exposure to toxic chemicals following the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio, train derailment indicated that the incident could have put thousands of Americans at risk, according to documents obtained by a watchdog group.

The incident, which became a political flashpoint, spilled chemicals including vinyl chloride , which is used to make plastic, into the town near the border with Pennsylvania.

Vinyl chloride can break down into other potentially harmful chemicals phosgene and hydrogen chloride .

The government projected in the days following the accident that exposure to those two substances could pose significant harm, the documents obtained by the Government Accountability Project reveal.

The day after the train derailment, the federal Interagency Modeling and Atmospheric Assessment Center projected that 17,972 people may be exposed to phosgene and 312 may be exposed to hydrogen chloride at levels “that could possibly result in at least severe injury.”

It projected that 1,901 people could be exposed to phosgene and 185 could be exposed to hydrogen chloride at “hazard levels that could possibly result in death.”

It does not appear that those figures were revealed to the public, though people living nearby the derailment were ordered to evacuate .

In the hours and days that followed, the interagency model projected that dramatically fewer people were at risk.

Nevertheless, critics say that the government should have informed the public about the initial projections.

“The government modeled thousands of casualties, then buried the maps and let residents walk back into the plume,” Lesley Pacey, senior environmental officer at Government Accountability Project, said in a written statement.

“It took a whistleblower declaration and six federal agency FOIA requests before DOD [Department of Defense] produced what the public should have been told from the beginning,” Pacey said.

Asked about the projections, a spokesperson for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said that its personnel were on-site “within hours of the derailment.”

“We remained transparent to provide the community with the most up-to-date information via our website, welcome center, community meetings, newsletter and more. EPA continues to provide information to residents about long-term site monitoring,” said the spokesperson, who did not sign their name to the statement.

The spokesperson added that the initial model, which was created at the agency’s request, “assessed an absolute worst-case scenario” and said that as it collected more information, the government produced updated models.

They said that the models were shared with state and local officials.

A spokesperson for the Federal Emergency Management Agency said that the agency “cannot speculate on prior officials’ motives, but communities facing hazardous materials incidents deserve timely, accurate, and transparent information.”

The spokesperson, who also did not sign their name to the statement, described the incident as “yet another Biden cover up at the expense of the American people” saying “these documents raise serious questions about what the Biden Administration knew, when it knew it, and why the public was not given the full picture.”

Dan Tierney, spokesperson for Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) said in an email that the projections were made before the evacuation was ordered and said that evacuating the area “would have dramatically reduced any potential impact.”

Tierney added that subsequent modeling “did not show widespread areas affected at a level that would suggest serious health consequences.”

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s (D) office said that since the derailment occurred in Ohio, Pennsylvania did not have jurisdiction over the site. The Shapiro administration noted that the modeling was an initial worst-case scenario and that later modeling showed more limited impacts.

The incident became highly politicized, as President Trump lambasted the Biden administration’s handling of it and criticized then-President Biden for not visiting the town until a year later .

The Biden administration had defended its actions and blamed Republicans for lax regulations .

articles.title: Hegseth considering Pentagon chief spokesperson to replace Army secretary
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is considering his chief spokesperson, Sean Parnell, to succeed Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who is eyeing an exit from the Pentagon in the coming months, two sources familiar with the matter told The Hill. The Hill previously reported that Parnell, who is also one of Hegseth’s senior advisers, has privately expressed…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is considering his chief spokesperson, Sean Parnell, to succeed Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who is eyeing an exit from the Pentagon in the coming months, two sources familiar with the matter told The Hill.

The Hill previously reported that Parnell, who is also one of Hegseth’s senior advisers, has privately expressed his interest in the role.

In response to questions to Parnell, a senior administration official told The Hill that he is “100 percent focused on the job he was appointed to by President Trump and Secretary Hegseth.”

A Pentagon official and former official familiar with the internal deliberations said he’s on Hegseth’s short list of candidates to replace Driscoll.

“Mr. Parnell has a deep bench of supporters throughout the Administration and has worked tirelessly to enable cultural change and accountability in the Pentagon,” the Pentagon official said in a statement to The Hill.

“Leveraging his extensive combat and executive experience, he will bring the accountability, change, and engaged transformational leadership the Army so desperately needs at this time.”

The White House referred questions about Parnell’s future to the Pentagon.

Driscoll is looking to depart his role around the end of the year following a months-long influence battle with Hegseth, The Hill reported last week .

The Army secretary is open to resigning “around” Labor Day, but the White House wants him to stay at least through the November midterms, according to one source familiar with the deliberations, confirming an NBC News report published Tuesday.

Driscoll’s spokesperson declined to comment. NBC News reported the Army secretary was at the White House on Monday to discuss his future.

Parnell, who is also the chair of the Afghanistan Withdrawal Special Review Panel, has served as the top Pentagon spokesperson since February last year.

Prior to his stint at the Pentagon, Parnell, who was awarded two Bronze Stars and a Purple Heart for his service during the Afghanistan War, ran for Congress twice.

Parnell was endorsed by President Trump during his Senate run in Pennsylvania, but withdrew from the race in November 2021 after losing a court fight over custody of his three children. The judge in that case said he believed allegations of abuse by Parnell’s estranged wife. Parnell has denied the allegations.

In 2020, Parnell lost to Connor Lamb for Pennsylvania’s 17th district House of Representatives seat.

articles.title: Hegseth upgrades medals of three Marines who survived Afghanistan attack five years ago
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday upgraded the valor awards of three Marines who guarded the Abbey Gate at the Hamid Karzai International Airport when a bomb went off as U.S. service members were evacuating from Afghanistan five years ago. The Marines — Gunnery Sgt. Jonathan Eby, Cpl. Michael Gretzon, Lance Cpl. Jordan Houston —were…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday upgraded the valor awards of three Marines who guarded the Abbey Gate at the Hamid Karzai International Airport when a bomb went off as U.S. service members were evacuating from Afghanistan five years ago.

The Marines — Gunnery Sgt. Jonathan Eby, Cpl. Michael Gretzon, Lance Cpl. Jordan Houston —were aiding with security on Aug. 26, 2021, the day a suicide bomber struck the gate and killed 13 service members and 170 Afghans.

At a ceremony at the Pentagon, Hegseth marked the five-year anniversary of the tragedy by awarding the Bronze Star Medal with a “V” device for valor to Houston and Eby, and the Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medal with a “V” device to Gretzon.

“They stood in the direct blast zone with minimal cover, fully aware of an imminent suicide threat,” he said. “Yet they stayed on that line because they knew that their brothers in arms and thousands of innocents depended on them.”

The Pentagon’s Afghanistan Withdrawal Special Review Panel earlier this year recommended the upgraded awards over the original awards which “did not reflect” the danger the Abbey Gate location posed and the service members’ heroic actions.

Hegseth last year ordered a review into the U.S. evacuation from Afghanistan as the country fell to Taliban control. The Trump administration has placed blame at the feet of former President Joe Biden for the chaotic and deadly evacuation of American citizens and Afghans who had aided the U.S. government in the country’s nearly 20-year war.

Most assessments, however, have concluded blame is shared between President Trump and Biden — Trump for signing a 2020 deal with the Taliban to withdraw all American forces and Biden for announcing he would proceed with the pullout, setting off panic as Afghan forces abandoned their posts, allowing the Taliban to sweep into Kabul.

Hegseth took Wednesday’s ceremony to bash the prior administration for allowing “bureaucratic caution, or maybe politics, to stand in the way of proper recognition.”

“A military that downplays its frontline heroes to avoid uncomfortable political truths only projects weakness,” Hegseth said. “For too long, leadership in this capital city failed to match that frontline courage with administrative backbone, inappropriately downgrading the original award submissions that these men rightfully deserved,” he said of the Marines.

Earlier on Wednesday, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell announced that classified documents had been discovered during a review of the Kabul airport attack, which he claimed were “stashed and hidden away in safes where they would not be found.”

Parnell, who is chairman of the Afghanistan Withdrawal Special Review Panel, did not provide details about the contents of the newly discovered papers, only saying that they were “highly relevant classified documents” and “material that should have been disclosed.”

After his team reviewed the documents “it became clear why someone would try to hide them,” he added.

“I’m not going to give you a convenient version of the truth, nor will I give you a rushed one,” Parnell said in a video message posted to X. “We are following the evidence to wherever it leads and to whoever it touches.”

articles.body:
Do Iran’s latest threats to Europe have teeth?

Iran’s recent saber-rattling against Bulgaria has renewed questions over how much it’s willing to directly attack Europe in an effort to deter U.S. allies from aiding war efforts.

Bulgaria, among Iran’s biggest trading partners in Eastern Europe, is among the European countries Iran considered striking if President Trump escalated the war, The Financial Times reported last week. That’s due to both its south-eastern location on the continent and two U.S. Air Force KC-135 refueling planes using one of its bases to support Operation Epic Fury.

After Bulgarian officials announced the departure of those planes over the weekend, Iran on Monday issued its latest warning to NATO members that allow their territory to be a jumping off point for American or Israeli military action against the regime, saying it “ has the right to target the point of origin and source of any act of aggression against” it.

Iran has made similar threats to the United Kingdom , with a drone striking a British airbase in Cyprus in March. That same month, Iran fired two ballistic missiles at the remote U.K.-U.S. base in the Indian Ocean known as Diego Garcia. And Turkey in March said NATO’s air defenses had intercepted several ballistic missiles launched from Iran.

While Iran clearly wants to maintain the perception that it’s willing and capable of striking Europe, analysts aren’t convinced it really wants to invite NATO more fully into the fight.

“I don’t think the juice is worth the squeeze in terms of antagonizing NATO. . . . I don’t think that attacking European targets gets them anything extra than attacking [Gulf] targets doesn’t get them,” said Alan Eyre, a former head of the Iran office at the U.S. Consulate in Dubai, now with the Middle East Institute.

David Cattler, a senior fellow with the Center for European Policy Analysis, likewise said that an Iranian strike on a NATO ally would be a major escalation but a bad strategic trade for Tehran , as “that would probably transform Europeans who largely have sought distance from the Iran war into active participants against” the regime.

He said the more immediate issue is Iranian coercion.

“The reality is Tehran doesn’t need to fire a missile at Bulgaria to achieve an effect . Threatening the countries that provide the bases, logistic support, access to the United States is itself an attempt to raise the price of supporting Washington in an attempt to weaken allied cohesion,” Cattle told The Hill.

articles.title: Flock contract cancellations grow among cities, other jurisdictions
articles.summary: Two Phoenix, Ariz. suburbs became the latest municipalities Wednesday to terminate their contracts with Flock Safety, cancelling their use of the company’s automated license plate readers (ALPRs) that have drawn widespread privacy concerns. The city of Tempe, which had an $80,000 contract with the company, said it would turn off all of its Flock cameras…
articles.body:
Two Phoenix, Ariz. suburbs became the latest municipalities Wednesday to terminate their contracts with Flock Safety , cancelling their use of the company’s automated license plate readers (ALPRs) that have drawn widespread privacy concerns.

The city of Tempe, which had an $80,000 contract with the company, said it would turn off all of its Flock cameras due to mounting reports of data “misuse” in other regions. Three hours later, the nearby town of Cave Creek also announced it had ended its contract with Flock and completely removed the technology.

“While the cameras have been a useful tool for Tempe … recent cases involving the misuse of automated license plate reader systems in Arizona and nationwide have raised concerns about the risks that come with the technology,” Tempe wrote in a press release posted to social platform X.

The nearby town similarly wrote on X, “In light of several high-profile abuse cases reported locally and nationally, as well as a recent theft of a FLOCK camera … staff determined it was in the best interest of the community to discontinue the system.”

Flock offers a system able to recognize license plates immediately. The technology uses cameras and audio devices to record plate numbers, as well as identify what the company calls a “vehicle signature.” Though ALPRs do not collect any biometric data or facial recognition.

The company then shares vehicle information with other law enforcement agencies, creating a large network — more than 120,000 cameras in 49 states — to help solve crimes.

Over 90 cities, according to anti-surveillance organization DeFlock , have made moves to cancel or reject Flock license plate camera readers as of Wednesday.

An early August Washington Post investigation found more than 50 law enforcement officers had been accused, charged with or convicted of misusing ALPRs for unauthorized purposes — including to stalk past partners without their consent.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called the increasing use of ALPRs “out of control” during a Wednesday press conference.

“I’m all about having law enforcement have tools to be able to hold criminals accountable,” DeSantis said, according to ABC7 Sarasota . “But I don’t want to have this become a surveillance state.”

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) also launched an investigation Wednesday into Flock’s national surveillance network, naming multiple instances of “abuse and misuse of personal data.”

In his letter to Flock CEO Garrett Langley, Hawley cited a February case where a police officer allegedly searched his ex-girlfriend’s license plate number 124 times and her former boyfriend’s plate 55 times.

Flock announced changes to its privacy and data retention policies last week amid a growing number of lawsuits. It now requires agencies to implement an “Audit Assistance” feature, which spots abnormal activity and flags it for administrator review.

The policy changes also included a “proactive lockout” feature that automatically suspends access to Flock data if a user’s activity meets a threshold for abnormal behavior pending administrator review.

The American Civil Liberties Union, which has several pending cases against Flock, said the policy “seems positive at first blush,” but “the devil will be in the details” of its actual functionality.

A Flock spokesperson told The Hill Wednesday that, while the company respected the city of Tempe’s decision, it still maintains that the technology keeps communities safe.

“We believe Tempe could have preserved the system’s value in helping solve serious crimes while still respecting privacy, and taking that tool away does not make a community safer,” the spokesperson said.

This story was updated at 9:03 p.m. on Aug. 26, 2026.

articles.title: ATF investigates ‘major’ cybersecurity incident as ransomware group claims attack
articles.summary: The ATF is investigating a cybersecurity incident designated a "major incident" by Justice Department officials as Qilin ransomware claims credit.
articles.body: The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) said Wednesday it is investigating a cybersecurity incident involving a standalone system, which senior Justice Department officials have designated a "major incident" under federal guidelines. The disclosure comes as the Qilin ransomware group claimed ATF as a victim, according to cybersecurity outlets tracking the group's leak site. The group has not publicly provided evidence substantiating its claim, and the ATF has not attributed the incident to Qilin. The ATF said the affected system operates separately from its enterprise network and that there is no indication the incident affected the agency's broader network, its eForms system or any other ATF system. The agency disconnected the affected environment after discovering the incident and launched forensic and incident-response efforts. The ATF is coordinating with the Justice Department as it investigates what happened. FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS The agency did not identify the affected system, say when the incident was discovered or disclose whether any data was accessed or stolen. Cybernews reported Wednesday that Qilin claimed ATF as its latest victim but had provided no evidence or details supporting the claim. GalaxyWarden, a breach-monitoring service, separately reported that ATF appeared on Qilin's leak site and that the group claimed it obtained files from the agency. GalaxyWarden said it had not independently verified the group's assertions. Fox News Digital reached out to the ATF and the Justice Department for additional information, including whether officials believe Qilin was responsible for the incident, whether any data was accessed or stolen and what prompted officials to designate the event a "major incident." The ATF said senior Justice Department officials designated the cybersecurity event a "major incident" under applicable federal guidelines and that required notifications have been completed. articles.title: NASA administrator suggests putting data centers in space
articles.summary: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman on Wednesday suggested housing data centers in space amid mounting controversy surrounding the facilities’ growing presence in the U.S. “Let’s take our data centers, put them in Earth orbit, take advantage of that free fusion reactor that’s out there for us and use that to ensure we do win the ……
articles.body:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman on Wednesday suggested housing data centers in space amid mounting controversy surrounding the facilities’ growing presence in the U.S.

“Let’s take our data centers, put them in Earth orbit, take advantage of that free fusion reactor that’s out there for us and use that to ensure we do win the … space race for sure, but the (artificial intelligence) race, too,” Isaacman said in an interview with Nexstar DC’s Vinay Simot.

He added that the move would “have immense benefits,” as companies could leverage solar energy — the aforementioned “free fusion reactor” — to power data centers.

Data centers, which fuel the growing artificial intelligence (AI) industry, have quickly lost favor with the public — with many saying their presence raises prices in communities and carries negative environmental impacts.

Amid this pushback , both Democratic and Republican politicians are hastily trying to distance themselves from the facilities. Some swing state candidates have backed stricter policy on data centers, alleging their opponents are too close with the tech industry.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) signed an order last week requiring that data center developers cover electricity costs and gain local backing for projects. Shapiro had previously boasted about these facilities’ investments in his state.

Wednesday was not the first time the NASA administrator proposed the idea of sending data centers into space. In an early August appearance on the New York Post’s “Pod Force One” podcast, Isaacman called the proposal a “fantastic” solution to the publics’ complaints.

“Elon [Musk] and others in the industry are like, ‘Let’s take the data centers that no one likes in your backyard — it seems like there’s a lot of consensus on that — and put them into space where they won’t bother anyone’,” Isaacman said during the podcast.

He added that the space data centers would need solar panels “the size of several football fields.”

Although some lawmakers have called for data center bans, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin on Sunday advised against the idea — pointing to possible ramifications for the U.S. in its AI race against China.

“There’s been a push from some states where they’re talking about a statewide moratorium , and what I’ve found is that most of this country wants to make sure the United States wins this race to be the AI capital of the world, that we do not relinquish this to China,” Zeldin said during an appearance on John Catsimatidis’s radio show “The Cats Roundtable” on 77 WABC.
